docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
minevent is a Python library that provides a minimal event system for Machine Learning. It allows you to customize code by adding pieces of code that are executed when an event is fired. minevent is organized around three main concepts:

  • event which defines the thing that should happen.
  • event handler which is a callable to execute when the event happens
  • event manager which is responsible to manage the events and event handlers.

The goal of this documentation is to explain how the event system works and how to use it. The library provides some implemented modules, but it is possible to extend it. It is possible to use all the components or just a subset based on the need. For example, a handler is a plain callable, so it can be tested without the event manager.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
minevent provides a minimal event system to customize a piece of code without changing its implementation. Below is an example on how to use minevent library.

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def say_something(manager: EventManager) -> None:
...     print("Hello, I am Bob!")
...     manager.trigger_event("after")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> say_something(manager)
Hello, I am Bob!
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("after", hello_handler)
>>> say_something(manager)
Hello, I am Bob!
Hello!

It allows you to customize the function say_something without changing its implementation. Please read the quickstart page to learn more about the library.

docs.title: API stability
docs.text: While minevent is in development stage, no API is guaranteed to be stable from one release to the next. In fact, it is very likely that the API will change multiple times before a stable 1.0.0 release. In practice, this means that upgrading minevent to a new version will possibly break any code that was using the old version of minevent.

docs.title: Architecture and Design Principles
docs.text: This page is the reference of the rules of minevent: the properties that it guarantees, the behaviors that it does not guarantee, the rule that calls the handlers and the reasons of the design. The quickstart is the first contact, the examples are runnable recipes and the user guide gives the recommendations.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
These properties hold for every release and each one is covered by tests.

# Property Statement Enforced by P1 Small surface Events are strings, handlers are plain callables, the manager connects them. Six exported names and __version__ (EventManager, Subscription, Context, Condition, PeriodicCondition, AfterNCondition). EventManager has 8 public members (events, get_subscriptions, add_event_handler, on, trigger_event, atrigger_event, clear_event, reset) and __len__, __contains__. test_init.py P2 Cheap import import minevent is cheap and has no side effect: standard library only, and not logging, inspect, asyncio or importlib.metadata, and it creates no typing object (NamedTuple, Protocol, TypeVar): the annotations are strings and the names that only a type checker needs are imported under TYPE_CHECKING (inspect is imported when the first handler is registered, the version on the first access of __version__). It starts no thread, reads no file, emits no warning and writes no log. test_import.py (modules and typing objects) P3 Events are strings An event name is a case-sensitive str; any other type raises TypeError. The empty string is valid. Reading the manager never creates an event. test_manager.py P4 Validated at the door add_event_handler and on reject, with a TypeError that names the argument and the value: a non-str event, a non-callable handler or condition, a signature that P13 rejects, and a generator or async generator function. A rejected registration leaves the manager unchanged. The annotations of a handler or a condition do not have to be resolvable. add_event_handler, _needs_context, test_manager.py P5 Registration identity add_event_handler returns a new Subscription every time; the same callable can be registered several times. remove() removes that registration only: True the first time, then False. active is True until the registration is removed, by whatever means. Subscription, test_manager.py P6 Registration order The handlers of an event run in the order they were registered, one after the other, in the calling thread. the ordered dict, test_manager.py P7 Snapshot dispatch A trigger visits the registrations that exist when it starts. A registration added by a running handler takes effect at the next trigger. A registration removed before its turn (by remove(), clear_event, reset or a once claim) does not run. Subscription._call, test_manager.py P8 Fail-fast with context An exception of a handler or a condition propagates unchanged (same object, same type); the remaining handlers are skipped. It carries a note with the event and the function of the handler (under a functools.partial), once per distinct pair. No message and no repr of the package runs the repr of user data to name a handler. _describe, _add_error_note, test_manager.py P9 once is at-most-once A once registration is removed by an atomic claim just before its handler is called, after its condition, so it is called at most once whatever the number of threads. A false or raising condition does not consume it; a handler that raises does. Subscription._call, test_manager_once.py, test_manager_threads.py P10 Synchronous by default trigger_event never awaits; a handler that returns an awaitable raises TypeError. atrigger_event awaits the handlers one after the other (an object with async def __call__ is a coroutine handler too). Conditions are synchronous in both: a condition that returns an awaitable raises TypeError. A coroutine that is rejected is closed. _check_not_awaitable, Subscription._call, test_manager_async.py P11 Thread-safe registry The registry is protected by a reentrant lock. Handlers, conditions and the repr of user objects run outside the lock, so a handler can use the manager. EventManager._lock, test_manager_threads.py P12 No hidden state No global manager, no discovery, no side effect of a read. Zero runtime dependency. A manager cannot be copied or pickled (copy.copy, copy.deepcopy and pickle raise the same TypeError). __reduce__, test_manager.py P13 Two calls A handler and a condition are called as f() or f(context). A parameter that has a default keeps it: the manager never fills it. A callable whose other parameters are none is called as f(); one with exactly one other parameter, positional, is called as f(context); any other signature (including *args and **kwargs), or one that cannot be inspected, is rejected (P4). Names and annotations are not checked. The signature is the one that inspect.signature reports, read once, at registration (the calling rule). _needs_context, test_manager.py P14 Payload is data trigger_event(event, context=None, /) copies the mapping context (a dict, for example), or reuses a Context as is, into one read-only Context per trigger, shared by the handlers and the conditions. A Context can be copied, deep-copied and pickled (protocol 2 or higher) if its values can; the values are not copied by the context itself. Any str key is allowed, it does not need to be a valid identifier. The handler decides what a missing key means (context[key] or context.get(key, default)). trigger_event, Context, test_context.py P15 Typed Fully typed, py.typed, ty check clean. The values of a Context are Any, so the documented handlers type check in the code of a user. ty check in CI, test_context_typing.py P16 Fast and linear About 0.3 µs for a trigger with one trivial handler, 0.1 µs for each extra one, 0.75 µs with a small dict (it is copied into a Context), and 4.5 µs for a registration plus its removal (the signature is inspected there, never in a trigger). Registering k handlers and removing them in any order costs O(k). Measured on a laptop with Python 3.14. tests/benchmarks/ P17 A manager is a service bool(manager) is always True, empty or not, so manager or default means "is there a manager". len(manager) is the number of registrations. __bool__, test_manager.py P18 One way to do each thing One way to register (add_event_handler, with on as its decorator form and the same keyword-only options once and condition), one way to adapt a callable (wrap it in a function, a lambda or a functools.partial that needs nothing or only the context), one way to run once (once=True), one way to extend (write a callable). No handler base class. One page states each rule. the signatures, the documents P19 Debuggable without a logger repr(subscription) names the event and the handler function (Subscription(event='epoch_end', handler='log_epoch')), repr(manager) counts the registrations per event. The library logs nothing: get_subscriptions(event) is the way to look. __repr__, test_manager.py P20 Everything that runs, is run Each pull request runs the unit and integration tests, the doctests, tests/package_checks.py and one pass of every benchmark (except the import benchmarks, which need the statistics and run on a schedule), so a change of the API cannot leave one of them behind. ci.yaml, test_package_checks.py

docs.title: The Calling Rule
docs.text:
A handler is written as def g() or def g(context: Context), and any callable that can be called in one of these two ways works: the parameters that have a default are ignored. The same rule applies to a condition, which returns a boolean. It is checked once, at registration.

Parameters without default Example Result none: no parameter def g() g() none: only positional with defaults model.train, lambda i=i: ... g() none: only keyword-only with defaults def g(*, v=1), partial(f, v=1) g() one, positional def g(context) g(context) one, positional, then defaults def g(context, verbose=False) g(context) *args, with or without **kwargs print, Mock(), AsyncMock() TypeError **kwargs def g(**kw) TypeError cannot be inspected max, dict.update TypeError two or more def g(a, b) TypeError one, keyword-only def g(*, epoch) TypeError (any) generator or async generator def g(): yield TypeError

Coroutine functions, bound methods, callable objects, classes and functools.partial objects follow the same table. The signature of a partial does not contain the arguments that it binds.

To adapt a callable, wrap it in a function, a lambda or a functools.partial:

manager.add_event_handler("epoch_start", model.train)  # model.train()
manager.add_event_handler("epoch_start", lambda: model.train(mode=True))  # a chosen value
manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda context: print(context))  # print the context
manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", functools.partial(save, "model.pt"))  # save(path, context)

In a test, unittest.mock.create_autospec(func) replaces Mock(): it has the signature of func.

A lambda created in a loop reads the loop variable when it is called, but a default value is evaluated when the lambda is created. So lambda i=i: print(i) saves the current value, and it is called without argument. A handler that needs a saved value and the context takes the context first, without default: lambda context, i=i: print(i, context["epoch"]).

docs.title: Not guaranteed
docs.text:
These behaviors are documented limits, not defects:

  • A removal in another thread. P7 is exact in the thread that triggers. A remove() from another thread cannot stop a handler that the trigger is about to call.
  • Recursion. A handler that triggers its own event recurses until RecursionError.
  • Blocking. A synchronous handler in atrigger_event blocks the event loop.
  • A callable object whose __call__ is a generator, and a function that returns a generator, do nothing. Only generator functions are rejected (P4) and awaitables detected (P10).
  • A coroutine handler registered with once=True and triggered with trigger_event is consumed: the TypeError is raised after the call.
  • An optional parameter never receives the context. def f(context=None) is called as f() and gets None, without an error: the context needs a parameter without default.
  • A decorated function is judged by the signature that inspect.signature reports: with functools.wraps, that is the signature of the wrapped function.
  • An exception class that forbids new attributes (a frozen=True dataclass exception) is replaced by the error of add_note.
  • A mutable value of the payload can be mutated by a handler, and the next ones see it.
  • Threads. The handlers run in the thread that triggers the event, concurrently if several threads trigger it, so a handler that shares state must protect it. The state of a condition (the counter of PeriodicCondition, for example) is not protected.
  • Prompt reclamation. A manager with registrations is in a reference cycle (manager, dict, Subscription, manager): del manager does not free it until the garbage collector runs. reset() releases the handlers at a known point.

docs.title: Design Notes
docs.text:
• Events are strings. They are easy to type, to read and to serialize. A namespace such as training.batch.end is a naming convention: there is no hierarchy.
  • A callable is the extension point. There is no base class to learn or to import. The introspection is limited to the signature at registration and to the awaitable results.
  • Synchronous and sequential. The handlers run in a deterministic order, which suits the sequential workflows of Machine Learning and is easy to debug. Coroutine handlers are opt-in with atrigger_event. The library starts no thread.
  • The registry maps each event to an ordered dict of subscriptions used as an ordered set, so a registration and a removal are O(1), and a trigger is linear in the handlers of the event. A reentrant lock protects it, and a trigger takes a snapshot under the lock and runs it outside.
  • The Subscription is the registration. It stores the handler and the options, so the same callable can be registered several times and each registration is removed on its own.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
minevent stays minimal. These features are not provided and are not planned:

  • Event objects with metadata or priorities: events are plain strings, and data is given as a dict (or a Context) to trigger_event.
  • Handler ordering other than the registration order.
  • Weak references or sender/receiver filtering.
  • Collecting handler errors: handlers run fail-fast, and an exception stops the dispatch. To run every handler and report all the failures, wrap the handler in a try/except (an ExceptionGroup option such as on_error="collect" was considered and declined to keep trigger_event minimal).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: This page shows how to use minevent in practical situations. The pycon examples run as written. The quickstart shows the basics, the user guide lists the recommendations and the architecture page states the rules.

docs.title: Add logging to a training loop
docs.text:
The training loop triggers events and knows nothing about the handlers. The caller decides what happens, so logging, checkpointing or monitoring is added without changing the loop:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def train(manager: EventManager, epochs: int) -> None:
...     manager.trigger_event("training_start")
...     for epoch in range(epochs):
...         loss = 1.0 / (epoch + 1)
...         manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": loss})
...     manager.trigger_event("training_end")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> train(manager, epochs=2)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_start", lambda: print("Training started"))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}: loss={context['loss']}")
... )
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", lambda: print("Training ended"))
>>> train(manager, epochs=2)
Training started
epoch 0: loss=1.0
epoch 1: loss=0.5
Training ended

The first call of train prints nothing because no handler is registered.

docs.title: Run a handler every N epochs
docs.text:
Give the registration a condition. PeriodicCondition(freq=3) is True on the first call and then every three calls; skip_first=True skips the first call:

>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda context: print(f"checkpoint at epoch {context['epoch']}"),
...     condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3, skip_first=True),
... )
>>> for epoch in range(7):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
checkpoint at epoch 3
checkpoint at epoch 6

AfterNCondition(n) is False for the first n calls, which is useful for a warm-up:

>>> from minevent import AfterNCondition, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda context: print(f"validate at epoch {context['epoch']}"),
...     condition=AfterNCondition(2),
... )
>>> for epoch in range(4):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
validate at epoch 2
validate at epoch 3

docs.title: Write a custom condition
docs.text:
A class with __call__ is useful when a condition has a state or reads another object:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> class Flag:
...     def __init__(self) -> None:
...         self.enabled = False
...
...     def __call__(self) -> bool:
...         return self.enabled
>>> verbose = Flag()
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda: print("batch done"), condition=verbose)
>>> manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
>>> verbose.enabled = True
>>> manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
batch done

docs.title: Combine conditions
docs.text:
Write a function. all([a(), b()]) evaluates every condition at each call, so stateful conditions advance together:

>>> from minevent import AfterNCondition, EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> after_one, periodic = AfterNCondition(1), PeriodicCondition(2)
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda: print("validate"),
...     condition=lambda: all([after_one(), periodic()]),
... )
>>> for _ in range(5):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")
validate
validate

docs.title: Use one condition per handler
docs.text:
A stateful condition keeps its counter in the instance, so create one per registration, for example with a function:

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> def say(name: str) -> None:
...     print(name)
>>> def register(name: str) -> None:
...     manager.add_event_handler(
...         name, functools.partial(say, name), condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2)
...     )
>>> register("first")
>>> register("second")
>>> manager.trigger_event("first")
first
>>> manager.trigger_event("second")
second

docs.title: Decide from the payload
docs.text:
A condition with a parameter reads the payload of the trigger. A handler and its condition can read different keys:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def is_improving(context: Context) -> bool:
...     return context.get("loss", 1.0) < 0.5
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda context: print(f"save the model of epoch {context['epoch']}"),
...     condition=is_improving,
... )
>>> for epoch, loss in enumerate([0.9, 0.4, 0.6, 0.3]):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": loss})
save the model of epoch 1
save the model of epoch 3

The built-in conditions (PeriodicCondition, AfterNCondition) take no parameter. To combine one with a condition on the payload, write a function that calls it: condition=lambda context: periodic() and is_improving(context).

docs.title: Keep a state in a handler
docs.text:
A class with a __call__(self, context) method is a handler with its own state. This one collects the losses and is read after the training:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> class LossHistory:
...     def __init__(self) -> None:
...         self.losses = []
...
...     def __call__(self, context: Context) -> None:
...         self.losses.append(context["loss"])
>>> history = LossHistory()
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", history)
>>> for epoch, loss in enumerate([0.9, 0.6, 0.4]):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": loss})
>>> history.losses
[0.9, 0.6, 0.4]

The handler ignores the keys that it does not read, here epoch.

docs.title: Share an event between handlers with different needs
docs.text:
Each handler reads the keys that it needs and decides what to do with a missing one:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def log_loss(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"loss {context['loss']}")
>>> def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}, lr {context.get('lr', 0.1)}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", log_loss)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", log_epoch)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
loss 0.5
epoch 3, lr 0.1

docs.title: Register with a decorator
docs.text:
on registers a function and returns it unchanged, so the function can still be called directly. It takes the same options as add_event_handler:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> @manager.on("epoch_end", condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2))
... def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}")
>>> for epoch in range(3):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
epoch 0
epoch 2
>>> log_epoch(Context({"epoch": 10}))
epoch 10

docs.title: Pass a dict or a Context
docs.text:
A dict is copied and validated at each trigger, while a Context is passed as is, so build it once to reuse it:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}, loss {context['loss']}")
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
epoch 3, loss 0.5
>>> context = Context({"epoch": 4, "loss": 0.4})
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", context)
epoch 4, loss 0.4
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", context)
epoch 4, loss 0.4

docs.title: Bind fixed arguments
docs.text:
Use functools.partial for the arguments that do not come from the payload:

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def save(path: str, context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"save epoch {context['epoch']} to {path}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", functools.partial(save, "model.pt"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 4})
save epoch 4 to model.pt

docs.title: Register methods that have default arguments
docs.text:
A parameter that has a default keeps it, so a method such as model.train(mode=True) is registered as it is, and a lambda chooses another value. A default also saves the value of a loop variable:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> class Model:
...     def train(self, mode: bool = True) -> None:
...         print(f"train mode: {mode}")
>>> model = Model()
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_start", model.train)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("validation_start", lambda: model.train(mode=False))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_start", {"epoch": 0})
train mode: True
>>> manager.trigger_event("validation_start")
train mode: False
>>> for i in range(3):
...     _ = manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda i=i: print(i))
>>> manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
0
1
2

docs.title: Keep a snapshot of the payload
docs.text:
The values of a Context are not copied. copy.deepcopy takes a snapshot that the next handlers cannot change:

>>> import copy
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> snapshots = []
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", lambda context: snapshots.append(copy.deepcopy(context))
... )
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda context: context["losses"].append(0.1))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"losses": [0.5]})
>>> snapshots
[Context({'losses': [0.5]})]

docs.title: Run a handler once
docs.text:
once=True removes the registration just before its handler runs. With a condition, it waits for the first trigger where the condition is True:

>>> from minevent import AfterNCondition, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", lambda: print("saved"), once=True, condition=AfterNCondition(2)
... )
>>> for _ in range(4):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")
saved
>>> subscription.active
False

docs.title: Remove a handler
docs.text:
Keep the Subscription returned by add_event_handler to remove exactly that registration. A with block removes it when the block exits, which suits a handler that lives for one phase of the program:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> with manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda: print("profiling")):
...     manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
profiling
>>> manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
>>> len(manager)
0

manager.clear_event("batch_end") removes all the handlers of an event, and manager.reset() removes all the handlers of all the events, for example in a finally block at the end of a program.

docs.title: Register a handler only once
docs.text:
Registering the same handler twice runs it twice. Look at the registrations to add it only if it is not there:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> for _ in range(3):
...     if not any(s.handler is hello_handler for s in manager.get_subscriptions("my_event")):
...         _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> len(manager)
1

docs.title: Trace the handlers
docs.text:
Wrap a handler to see its calls. functools.wraps keeps the signature, which decides whether the handler receives the context:

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def traced(handler):
...     @functools.wraps(handler)
...     def wrapper(*args):
...         print(f"calling {handler.__name__}")
...         return handler(*args)
...     return wrapper
>>> def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", traced(log_epoch))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda context: print(dict(context)))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1})
calling log_epoch
epoch 1
{'epoch': 1}

docs.title: Write a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin registers its handlers when it is set up, and keeps the subscriptions to remove them when it is torn down:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> class ProgressPlugin:
...     def setup(self, manager: EventManager) -> None:
...         self.subscriptions = [
...             manager.add_event_handler("epoch_start", self.on_epoch_start),
...             manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", self.on_epoch_end),
...         ]
...
...     def teardown(self) -> None:
...         for subscription in self.subscriptions:
...             subscription.remove()
...
...     def on_epoch_start(self, context: Context) -> None:
...         print(f"start {context['epoch']}")
...
...     def on_epoch_end(self, context: Context) -> None:
...         print(f"end {context['epoch']}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> plugin = ProgressPlugin()
>>> plugin.setup(manager)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_start", {"epoch": 0})
start 0
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 0})
end 0
>>> plugin.teardown()
>>> len(manager)
0

docs.title: Use coroutine handlers
docs.text:
atrigger_event awaits the coroutine handlers and also runs the synchronous ones:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> async def notify(context: Context) -> None:
...     await asyncio.sleep(0)
...     print(f"notified epoch {context['epoch']}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}"))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", notify)
>>> asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1}))
epoch 1
notified epoch 1

docs.title: Trigger events from an async function
docs.text:
In an async program, await the trigger inside your coroutines. The next step starts when every handler is done:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> async def fetch_all(manager: EventManager, urls: list[str]) -> None:
...     await manager.atrigger_event("fetch_start", {"count": len(urls)})
...     for url in urls:
...         await asyncio.sleep(0)  # a real program awaits a request here
...         await manager.atrigger_event("fetch_done", {"url": url})
...     await manager.atrigger_event("fetch_end")
>>> async def log_done(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"fetched {context['url']}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "fetch_start", lambda context: print(f"fetching {context['count']} urls")
... )
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("fetch_done", log_done)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("fetch_end", lambda: print("done"))
>>> asyncio.run(fetch_all(manager, ["a.com", "b.com"]))
fetching 2 urls
fetched a.com
fetched b.com
done

docs.title: Use options with coroutine handlers
docs.text:
once, condition and the on decorator work the same way with coroutine handlers:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> @manager.on("epoch_end", condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2))
... async def upload(context: Context) -> None:
...     await asyncio.sleep(0)
...     print(f"uploaded epoch {context['epoch']}")
>>> async def main() -> None:
...     for epoch in range(3):
...         await manager.atrigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch, "loss": 0.5})
>>> asyncio.run(main())
uploaded epoch 0
uploaded epoch 2

docs.title: Run the work of a handler concurrently
docs.text:
The handlers of an event run sequentially, so a slow handler delays the next ones. To run several awaitables at the same time, use asyncio.gather inside one handler:

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> async def upload(name: str) -> str:
...     await asyncio.sleep(0)
...     return name
>>> async def upload_all(context: Context) -> None:
...     done = await asyncio.gather(*(upload(name) for name in context["files"]))
...     print(f"uploaded {done}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", upload_all)
>>> asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("training_end", {"files": ["a.pt", "b.pt"]}))
uploaded ['a.pt', 'b.pt']

Hand a long computation to an executor (await loop.run_in_executor(...) or asyncio.to_thread) from a coroutine handler.

docs.title: Handle an async handler used with trigger_event
docs.text:
trigger_event cannot await a coroutine, and raises a TypeError that names the handler:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> async def notify() -> None:
...     print("notified")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", notify)
>>> try:
...     manager.trigger_event("my_event")
... except TypeError as exc:
...     print(exc)
notify returned an awaitable; use atrigger_event

docs.title: Handle the errors of a handler
docs.text:
The exception of a handler reaches the caller with a note that names the event and the handler:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def fail() -> None:
...     raise ValueError("boom")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", fail)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", lambda: print("not reached"))
>>> try:
...     manager.trigger_event("my_event")
... except ValueError as exc:
...     print(exc, "|", exc.__notes__[0])
boom | raised by fail while handling the event 'my_event'

To keep the other handlers running, catch the exception in the handler.

docs.title: Test a handler
docs.text:
A handler is a plain callable, so test it without a manager. Test the wiring with a mock:

from unittest.mock import create_autospec

from minevent import Context, EventManager


def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
    print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}")


def test_epoch_end_calls_the_handler():
    manager = EventManager()
    handler = create_autospec(log_epoch)  # a mock with the signature of log_epoch
    manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", handler)
    manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1})
    handler.assert_called_once_with({"epoch": 1})

An async handler is tested with asyncio.run (or the async support of your test framework):

import asyncio
from unittest.mock import create_autospec

from minevent import Context, EventManager


async def upload(context: Context) -> None:
    await asyncio.sleep(0)


def test_epoch_end_awaits_the_handler():
    manager = EventManager()
    handler = create_autospec(upload)  # an async mock with the signature of upload
    manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", handler)
    asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1}))
    handler.assert_awaited_once_with({"epoch": 1})

docs.text: It is highly recommended to install in a virtual environment to keep your system in order.

docs.title: Installing with pip (recommended)
docs.text:
We highly recommend installing a virtual environment. minevent can be installed from pip using the following command:

pip install minevent

minevent has no dependency, so no optional dependencies or extras are required.

git clone git@github.com:durandtibo/minevent.git

uv venv --python 3.13
source .venv/bin/activate

Or if you're developing and need documentation dependencies:

docs.title: User guide
docs.text: This guide collects the recommendations, the pitfalls and the troubleshooting tips for using minevent. The quickstart shows the basics, the examples are the recipes, and the architecture page states the rules of the library.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
• Name the event after what happened, in the past tense: epoch_end, checkpoint_saved, not event1 or done.
  • Pick one convention for the whole project, for example snake_case (batch_end) or a namespace (training.batch.end). Names are only strings, so minevent has no notion of hierarchy.
  • Define the names in one place (constants or an Enum with str values) to avoid typos: the events "epoch_end" and "epoch-end" are different, and triggering an event without handler does nothing.

docs.title: Handlers and payload
docs.text:
• One handler does one thing (log, save, update a progress bar). Register the handlers of an event in the order they must run.
  • Pass the data of a trigger as a dict. Build a Context yourself to reuse it for several triggers: it is validated and copied only once.
  • Read an optional value with context.get(key, default), so that handlers with different needs can share an event.
  • Register a method or a function that has default arguments as it is, and wrap it in a lambda to choose a value (see the calling rule).
  • If the failure of a handler must not stop the program, catch the exception in the handler.
  • A synchronous handler that is slow blocks the caller (and the event loop in atrigger_event). Hand the work to an executor in the handler if the caller must not wait.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
• Give each registration its own PeriodicCondition or AfterNCondition: an instance shared by two handlers advances the same counter. Call reset() to restart it.
  • To combine conditions, write a function. lambda: a() and b() skips b when a is False, so use it when b is costly and stateless. lambda: all([a(), b()]) evaluates both, so stateful conditions advance together.
  • Use a condition to avoid the work of an expensive handler.

docs.title: The event manager
docs.text:
• Create the manager once and pass it where it is needed. minevent has no global manager on purpose: it keeps the tests independent and makes the ownership clear.
  • Keep the Subscription of a handler that you may remove. A registered handler lives as long as the manager (obj.method keeps obj alive, and so do the arguments of a functools.partial and the closures), and minevent uses no weak reference. Remove the subscriptions that you do not need any more with remove(), a with block, clear_event or reset.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Test a handler without a manager, and the wiring with create_autospec (see Test a handler).
  • Use a new EventManager in each test, or call manager.reset() if the manager is shared.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: The cost of a trigger is mostly the cost of the handlers (see P16 in the architecture page). To find a slow handler, time it or wrap it (see Trace the handlers).

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• A handler that triggers its own event recurses until RecursionError. Use a different event or a flag.
  • Registering the same handler twice runs it twice (see Register a handler only once).
  • Mutating a value of the payload: the values are not copied, so the next handlers see the change.
  • An optional parameter: def f(context=None) never receives the context.
  • Threads: a handler that shares state must protect it, and a stateful condition should be called from one thread.

docs.title: My handler does not run
docs.text:
1. The handler is registered for that event: manager.get_subscriptions("my_event").
  2. The event name matches exactly (case-sensitive).
  3. The condition returns True (a PeriodicCondition(freq=5) skips four calls out of five).
  4. It was not registered with once=True and already consumed: subscription.active is False.
  5. A handler of the same event ahead of it raised: the next handlers are skipped.

docs.title: KeyError: "key 'epoch' not found in the context; ..."
docs.text: The trigger did not give the key that the handler requires. The message lists the available keys. Give the key to the trigger, or read it as an optional value.

docs.title: TypeError: ... must need no argument or only the context
docs.text: The manager cannot call the handler or the condition with nothing or with the context only. Wrap it in a function or a lambda, or bind the extra arguments with functools.partial (see the calling rule).

docs.title: TypeError: ... must not be a generator function
docs.text: Calling a function with yield runs none of its code. Register a function that iterates over the generator.

docs.title: TypeError: condition ... returned an awaitable
docs.text: The condition is asynchronous. Compute the value before the trigger and pass it in the payload, or decide inside a coroutine handler.

docs.title: TypeError: ... returned an awaitable; use atrigger_event
docs.text: A coroutine handler was triggered with trigger_event. Call await manager.atrigger_event(...).

docs.title: subscription.remove() returns False
docs.text: The registration is already removed. This is not an error.

docs.title: Debug
docs.text: minevent does not log. print(manager) shows the number of handlers of each event, and manager.get_subscriptions(event) lists the registrations of an event with the name of each handler. To see the calls and the payload, trace the handlers.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
minevent has three concepts:

  • an event is a case-sensitive string that names something that happens;
  • an event handler is a callable that runs when the event happens;
  • an event manager stores the handlers and triggers the events.

This page shows how to register a handler, trigger an event, pass data and remove a handler. The examples show more recipes, and the architecture page states the rules of the library. To install it, see Get Started.

docs.title: Register a handler and trigger an event
docs.text:
Create an EventManager, add a handler to an event and trigger the event:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler() -> None:
...     print("Hello!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", hello_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("training_end")
Hello!

The manager has no global state: create one instance and pass it where it is needed. Triggering an event that has no handler does nothing. The handlers of an event run one after the other, in the order they were added:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", lambda: print("save the model"))
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("training_end", lambda: print("send a report"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("training_end")
save the model
send a report
>>> manager
EventManager(events={'training_end': 2})
>>> manager.events
['training_end']

The decorator on registers a function and returns it unchanged:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> @manager.on("training_start")
... def log_start() -> None:
...     print("start")
>>> manager.trigger_event("training_start")
start

docs.title: Pass data to the handlers
docs.text:
The second argument of trigger_event is the payload, a dict for example. A handler that has a parameter receives it in a read-only Context; a handler without parameter ignores it:

>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def log_epoch(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}, loss {context.get('loss', 'unknown')}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", log_epoch)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda: print("done"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1, "loss": 0.5})
epoch 1, loss 0.5
done
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 2})
epoch 2, loss unknown
done

context["epoch"] reads a required value and raises a KeyError if it is missing, and context.get("loss") reads an optional one. The arguments that do not come from the payload are bound with functools.partial:

>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> def save(path: str, context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"save epoch {context['epoch']} to {path}")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", functools.partial(save, "model.pt"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3})
save epoch 3 to model.pt

A handler needs no argument or only the context. A callable such as print is rejected when it is registered: wrap it in a function or a lambda (see the calling rule).

docs.title: Control when a handler runs
docs.text:
A condition is a function that returns a boolean: the handler runs only if it returns True. PeriodicCondition and AfterNCondition are provided, and a condition can read the payload:

>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end", lambda: print("checkpoint"), condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2)
... )
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda: print("late epoch"),
...     condition=lambda context: context["epoch"] >= 2,
... )
>>> for epoch in range(3):
...     manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": epoch})
checkpoint
checkpoint
late epoch

With once=True, a handler runs at most once:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda: print("first epoch"), once=True)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")
first epoch
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")

docs.title: Remove a handler
docs.text:
add_event_handler returns a Subscription, the registration of the handler. Its remove() method removes that registration only:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda: print("epoch"))
>>> subscription.remove()
True
>>> subscription.remove()
False
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end")

A with block removes the registration when it exits. clear_event removes all the handlers of an event, and reset removes all the handlers:

>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> with manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda: print("batch")):
...     manager.trigger_event("batch_end")
batch
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("batch_end", lambda: None)
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda: None)
>>> manager.clear_event("batch_end")
>>> manager.events
['epoch_end']
>>> manager.reset()
>>> len(manager)
0

docs.title: Coroutine handlers
docs.text:
Trigger an event with atrigger_event to await its coroutine handlers (trigger_event raises a TypeError for them):

>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> async def hello_handler(context: Context) -> None:
...     print(f"Hello {context['name']}!")
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("my_event", {"name": "John"}))
Hello John!

docs.title: minevent
docs.text:
Contain the main features of the minevent package.

minevent is a minimal event system with three concepts: an event (a case-sensitive string), a handler (a callable that needs no argument or only the context) and an event manager (EventManager) that stores the handlers and triggers the events.

  • EventManager.add_event_handler (or the on decorator) registers a handler and returns a Subscription, the registration itself, that removes exactly that registration.
  • EventManager.trigger_event runs the handlers in the order they were registered and passes its context argument (a mapping, the payload) to them in a read-only Context. EventManager.atrigger_event also awaits the coroutine handlers.
  • A condition is any function that returns a boolean, without parameter or with the Context of the trigger (Condition). PeriodicCondition and AfterNCondition are provided, and they control when a handler runs.

The package has no dependency, and __version__ is the version of the installed package.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", lambda context: print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}"))
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3})
epoch 3

docs.text:
Condition = Callable[[], bool] | Callable[[Context], bool]

A condition: a function that returns a boolean, without parameter or with the Context of the trigger.

docs.title: minevent.AfterNCondition
docs.text:
Implement a condition that is False for the first n calls and True afterwards.

The condition is stateful, like PeriodicCondition: each call advances the counter, so do not share one instance between several handlers, and call it from one thread because the counter is not protected by a lock. Use reset to restart the counter.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n int

The number of calls to skip. Must be a non-negative integer.

required

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if n is not an integer.

ValueError

if n is negative.

Example 
>>> from minevent import AfterNCondition
>>> condition = AfterNCondition(2)
>>> [condition() for _ in range(4)]
[False, False, True, True]

docs.title: minevent.AfterNCondition.n property
docs.text:
n: int

Get the number of skipped calls.

Returns:

Type Description int

The number of calls that evaluate to False.

docs.title: minevent.AfterNCondition.reset
docs.text:
reset() -> None

Reset the internal counter, as if the condition was just created.

Example 
>>> from minevent import AfterNCondition
>>> condition = AfterNCondition(1)
>>> condition(), condition()
(False, True)
>>> condition.reset()
>>> condition()
False

docs.title: minevent.Context
docs.text:
Bases: Mapping[str, 'Any']

Implement a read-only mapping of the payload of a trigger.

The data is copied at construction into a private dict, and a context has no method that changes it (no __setitem__, update or pop), so neither the code that built the context nor a handler can change what the next handler sees. The values themselves are not copied: a mutable value stays mutable. A context can be copied, deep-copied and pickled (with the protocol 2 or higher, like the default one) if its values can.

The values are typed Any: a type checker lets a handler use a value without a cast, and it does not check how the value is used.

context[key] reads a required value and raises a KeyError if it is missing. context.get(key, default) reads an optional value. key in context, len, iteration, keys, items, values and == are inherited from collections.abc.Mapping, so dict(context) is a valid **kwargs.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Mapping[str, object] | None

The mapping to copy, or None for an empty context. Default is None.

None

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if data is neither None nor a mapping, or if a key of data is not a str.

Example 
>>> from minevent import Context
>>> context = Context({"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
>>> context["epoch"]
3
>>> context.get("lr", 0.1)
0.1
>>> "loss" in context
True
>>> len(context)
2
>>> context
Context({'epoch': 3, 'loss': 0.5})
>>> import copy
>>> copy.deepcopy(context)
Context({'epoch': 3, 'loss': 0.5})

docs.title: minevent.EventManager
docs.text:
Implement an event manager.

This event manager allows registering event handlers and triggering events. An event is represented by a case-sensitive string. Each event can have multiple handlers attached, and all handlers are executed in the order they were added when the event is triggered.

add_event_handler (or the on decorator) registers an event handler and returns a Subscription that removes that registration. trigger_event runs the handlers synchronously, and atrigger_event awaits the coroutine handlers. The manager has no global state: create one instance and pass it where it is needed. Nothing is logged: to trace the registrations, read get_subscriptions(event), or wrap the handler. events, event in manager and len(manager) inspect the registry, and clear_event and reset empty it.

A handler is a callable that needs no argument or only the context. It is called as handler(context), with a read-only Context that holds the payload of the trigger, if it has a parameter without default, and as handler() otherwise: a parameter that has a default keeps it. The options of a registration (once and condition) are the keyword-only arguments of add_event_handler and on. Use functools.partial, a function or a lambda to give other arguments.

Error policy: handlers run fail-fast. If a handler raises, the exception propagates to the caller of trigger_event (or atrigger_event) and the remaining handlers of that event are not executed.

Thread safety: the registration, removal and inspection of handlers are protected by a reentrant lock, and trigger_event runs the handlers on a snapshot taken under the lock, outside of it. So handlers can be registered in one thread and events triggered from worker threads. The handlers themselves run in the thread that triggers the event, concurrently if several threads trigger the same event, so a handler that shares state must be thread-safe. The mutable state of a condition, such as the counter of PeriodicCondition, is not protected.

A manager is a service, not a collection: bool(manager) is always True, even when it has no handler, so manager or default means "is there a manager". Use len(manager) for the number of registrations. A manager owns a lock and a registry, so it cannot be copied or pickled (copy.copy, copy.deepcopy and pickle raise a TypeError): create a new one.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler():
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> bool(manager)
True
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!

docs.text:
events: list[str]

Get the events that have at least one registered handler.

Returns:

Type Description list[str]

The event names, in the order they were first registered.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> manager.events
[]
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", lambda: None)
>>> manager.events
['my_event']
>>> "my_event" in manager
True

docs.title: minevent.EventManager.add_event_handler
docs.text:
add_event_handler(
    event: str,
    handler: Callable[..., object],
    *,
    once: bool = False,
    condition: Condition | None = None,
) -> Subscription

Add a handler to an event.

The handler will be called every time the specified event is triggered, as handler() or handler(context), where context is the read-only Context built from the payload of the trigger. A parameter that has a default keeps it: the manager never fills it. If no other parameter is left, the handler is called as handler(); if exactly one positional parameter is left, it is called as handler(context); and any other signature is rejected, including *args, **kwargs and a signature that cannot be inspected. This is checked once, at registration, and it never matches names or annotations. Wrap a rejected callable, such as print, in a function or a lambda. Multiple handlers can be registered to the same event, and they will be executed in the order they were added. Use functools.partial to bind other arguments.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default event str

The event name (case-sensitive string) to which the handler should be attached.

required handler Callable[..., object]

The callable to attach to the event.

required once bool

If True, the handler is removed just before its first execution, so it runs at most once, even when several threads trigger the event. A condition that is False does not consume the registration: it waits for the first time the condition is True. Default is False.

False condition Condition | None

An optional condition: a synchronous function that returns a boolean (a condition that returns an awaitable, such as a coroutine function, makes the trigger raise a TypeError). It is called each time the event is triggered, before the handler, and the handler runs only if it returns True. It is called as condition() or condition(context), with the rule of the handlers: a parameter that has a default keeps it. If None, the handler always runs. An exception raised by the condition propagates to the caller of trigger_event. A stateful condition, such as PeriodicCondition, must not be shared between registrations. Default is None.

None

Returns:

Type Description Subscription

A subscription whose remove method removes this registration only.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if event is not a string, if handler is not callable, if condition is neither None nor callable, or if handler or condition is a generator function, needs another argument than the context, or has a signature that cannot be inspected. The manager is unchanged.

Example 
>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> def hello_handler():
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> subscription.remove()
True
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler, once=True)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
>>> def greet_handler(message):
...     print(message)
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "greet", functools.partial(greet_handler, "Hello!")
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("greet")
Hello!
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "tick", hello_handler, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2)
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("tick")
Hello!
>>> manager.trigger_event("tick")
>>> def epoch_handler(context):
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}")
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", epoch_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
epoch 3

docs.title: minevent.EventManager.atrigger_event async
docs.text:
atrigger_event(
    event: str, context: Mapping[str, object] | None = None
) -> None

Trigger the handler(s) for the given event, awaiting the coroutine handlers.

This method behaves like trigger_event, but the handlers that are coroutine functions (or return an awaitable) are awaited. Synchronous handlers can be mixed with coroutine handlers. The handlers run one after the other, in the order they were added, and they are fail-fast like in trigger_event: the exception is not wrapped and has a note with the event and the handler. The snapshot of the handlers, the once registrations and the context follow the rules of trigger_event. Synchronous handlers block the event loop while they run.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default event str

The event name (case-sensitive string) to trigger.

required context Mapping[str, object] | None

The data passed to the handlers: a mapping from str to values, a Context or None. It is not modified. Default is None.

None

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if event is not a string, if context is neither None nor a mapping with str keys, or if a condition returns an awaitable (the conditions are synchronous and are never awaited). Any exception raised by a handler or a condition also propagates.

Example 
>>> import asyncio
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> async def hello_handler(context):
...     print(f"Hello {context['name']}!")
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> asyncio.run(manager.atrigger_event("my_event", {"name": "John"}))
Hello John!

reset() -> None

Reset the event manager.

This method removes all registered event handlers from the event manager, so their subscriptions become inactive. After calling this method, the event manager returns to its initial state. A registration that has not run yet in a running trigger does not run.

Example 
>>> # Create an event manager
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> # Add an event handler
>>> def hello_handler():
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> len(manager)
1
>>> # Reset the event manager
>>> manager.reset()
>>> len(manager)
0

docs.title: minevent.EventManager.trigger_event
docs.text:
trigger_event(
    event: str, context: Mapping[str, object] | None = None
) -> None

Trigger the handler(s) for the given event.

This method executes all event handlers registered for the specified event in the order they were added. Nothing happens if no handler is registered.

Handlers are executed fail-fast: if a handler raises, the exception propagates and the remaining handlers are skipped. The exception is not wrapped: it has a note (__notes__) with the event and the function of the handler that raised it.

The handlers are read from a snapshot taken when the event is triggered. A handler added by a running handler takes effect on the next trigger. A registration removed before its turn (by remove, clear_event or reset) does not run. A once registration is removed just before its handler runs.

A handler can trigger events, including the event it handles, but nothing stops the recursion: a handler that always triggers its own event raises a RecursionError. Guard the recursive trigger with a condition or a flag.

The data context (a mapping from str to values, a Context or None) is copied into one read-only Context that is built once per trigger and shared by all the handlers. A Context is passed as is (it is immutable, so it can be reused for several triggers), and None means no data. A handler that has a parameter without default is called as handler(context), and the other handlers are called as handler() (see add_event_handler). A handler reads the keys it needs and decides what to do when one is missing: context["key"] raises a KeyError, and context.get("key", default) returns a default. Extra keys never break a handler. The keys can be any str, they do not need to be valid identifiers. All the handlers receive the same value objects.

Before its handler, a registration evaluates its condition (the handler is skipped if it is False), and a once registration is removed.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default event str

The event name (case-sensitive string) to trigger.

required context Mapping[str, object] | None

The data passed to the handlers: a mapping from str to values, a Context or None. It is not modified. Default is None.

None

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if event is not a string, if context is neither None nor a mapping with str keys, if a condition returns an awaitable, or if a handler returns an awaitable (use atrigger_event for coroutine handlers). Any exception raised by a handler or a condition also propagates, including a RecursionError if a handler always triggers its own event.

Example 
>>> from minevent import Context, EventManager
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")  # do nothing because there is no event handler
>>> def hello_handler():
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> def epoch_handler(context):
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}")
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", epoch_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3})
epoch 3
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", Context({"epoch": 4}))
epoch 4

docs.title: minevent.PeriodicCondition
docs.text:
Implement a periodic condition.

This condition evaluates to True on the first call and then every freq calls. It maintains an internal counter that increments with each call. The condition is True when the counter modulo freq equals zero.

Note that a call is not idempotent: each call advances the counter, so the condition is stateful. Do not share one instance between several handlers, because they would advance the same counter. Use reset to restart the counter. The counter is not protected by a lock, so a condition should be called from one thread.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default freq int

The frequency (interval) at which the condition evaluates to True. Must be a positive integer.

required skip_first bool

If True, the first call evaluates to False, and then the condition evaluates to True every freq calls. Default is False.

False

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if freq is not an integer.

ValueError

if freq is lower than 1.

Example 
>>> from minevent import PeriodicCondition
>>> condition = PeriodicCondition(freq=3)
>>> [condition() for _ in range(7)]
[True, False, False, True, False, False, True]
>>> condition = PeriodicCondition(freq=2, skip_first=True)
>>> [condition() for _ in range(3)]
[False, False, True]

docs.title: minevent.Subscription
docs.text:
Represent the registration of a handler to an event.

A subscription is returned by EventManager.add_event_handler. It is the registration itself: the manager stores it with the options of the registration, and it removes exactly the registration that created it. The handler does not need to be re-created to be unsubscribed, other registrations of the same handler are not removed, and registering the same handler twice creates two independent subscriptions. Subscriptions are compared by identity.

A subscription is a context manager: the registration is removed when the with block exits.

The constructor is internal: subscriptions are created by the event manager.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default manager EventManager

The event manager that stores the registration.

required event str

The event name of the registration.

required handler Callable[..., object]

The registered handler: a callable.

required once bool

If True, the registration is removed just before its first execution. Default is False.

False condition Condition | None

The condition evaluated before the handler, or None if the handler always runs. It is called with the context if it has a parameter without default. Default is None.

None

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if the signature of handler or condition is rejected (see EventManager.add_event_handler).

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler():
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> subscription.event
'my_event'
>>> subscription.handler is hello_handler
True
>>> subscription.active
True
>>> subscription.remove()
True
>>> subscription.remove()
False
>>> subscription.active
False
>>> manager.events
[]
>>> with manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler):
...     manager.events
...
['my_event']
>>> manager.events
[]

docs.title: minevent.conditions
docs.text:
Implement some conditions that can be used in the event system.

A condition is any function that returns a boolean: a lambda, a method, or an object with a __call__(self) -> bool method like the conditions of this module. It is called as condition(), or as condition(context) with the read-only Context of the trigger if it has a parameter without default, so it can depend on the payload: lambda context: context.get("epoch", 0) > 5. Like a handler, it keeps the values of the parameters that have a default, and any other signature is rejected at registration. A condition is synchronous, in atrigger_event too: the trigger raises a TypeError if it returns an awaitable. Condition is the type alias Callable[[], bool] | Callable[[Context], bool]. A condition is called each time the event is triggered, before the handler, and the handler is executed only if it returns True. A condition can keep a state between calls. The built-in conditions take no parameter.

To combine conditions, write a function. The function decides which conditions are evaluated: lambda: a() and b() skips b when a is False, while lambda: all([a(), b()]) evaluates both, so stateful conditions advance together.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "hello", lambda: print("Hello!"), condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=3)
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("hello")
Hello!
>>> manager.trigger_event("hello")
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("bye", lambda: print("Bye!"), condition=lambda: False)
>>> manager.trigger_event("bye")
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "epoch_end",
...     lambda: print("late epoch"),
...     condition=lambda context: context.get("epoch", 0) >= 2,
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 1})
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 2})
late epoch

docs.title: minevent.context.Context
docs.text:
Bases: Mapping[str, 'Any']

Implement a read-only mapping of the payload of a trigger.

The data is copied at construction into a private dict, and a context has no method that changes it (no __setitem__, update or pop), so neither the code that built the context nor a handler can change what the next handler sees. The values themselves are not copied: a mutable value stays mutable. A context can be copied, deep-copied and pickled (with the protocol 2 or higher, like the default one) if its values can.

The values are typed Any: a type checker lets a handler use a value without a cast, and it does not check how the value is used.

context[key] reads a required value and raises a KeyError if it is missing. context.get(key, default) reads an optional value. key in context, len, iteration, keys, items, values and == are inherited from collections.abc.Mapping, so dict(context) is a valid **kwargs.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Mapping[str, object] | None

The mapping to copy, or None for an empty context. Default is None.

None

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if data is neither None nor a mapping, or if a key of data is not a str.

Example 
>>> from minevent import Context
>>> context = Context({"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
>>> context["epoch"]
3
>>> context.get("lr", 0.1)
0.1
>>> "loss" in context
True
>>> len(context)
2
>>> context
Context({'epoch': 3, 'loss': 0.5})
>>> import copy
>>> copy.deepcopy(context)
Context({'epoch': 3, 'loss': 0.5})

docs.title: minevent.manager.EventManager
docs.text:
Implement an event manager.

This event manager allows registering event handlers and triggering events. An event is represented by a case-sensitive string. Each event can have multiple handlers attached, and all handlers are executed in the order they were added when the event is triggered.

add_event_handler (or the on decorator) registers an event handler and returns a Subscription that removes that registration. trigger_event runs the handlers synchronously, and atrigger_event awaits the coroutine handlers. The manager has no global state: create one instance and pass it where it is needed. Nothing is logged: to trace the registrations, read get_subscriptions(event), or wrap the handler. events, event in manager and len(manager) inspect the registry, and clear_event and reset empty it.

A handler is a callable that needs no argument or only the context. It is called as handler(context), with a read-only Context that holds the payload of the trigger, if it has a parameter without default, and as handler() otherwise: a parameter that has a default keeps it. The options of a registration (once and condition) are the keyword-only arguments of add_event_handler and on. Use functools.partial, a function or a lambda to give other arguments.

Error policy: handlers run fail-fast. If a handler raises, the exception propagates to the caller of trigger_event (or atrigger_event) and the remaining handlers of that event are not executed.

Thread safety: the registration, removal and inspection of handlers are protected by a reentrant lock, and trigger_event runs the handlers on a snapshot taken under the lock, outside of it. So handlers can be registered in one thread and events triggered from worker threads. The handlers themselves run in the thread that triggers the event, concurrently if several threads trigger the same event, so a handler that shares state must be thread-safe. The mutable state of a condition, such as the counter of PeriodicCondition, is not protected.

A manager is a service, not a collection: bool(manager) is always True, even when it has no handler, so manager or default means "is there a manager". Use len(manager) for the number of registrations. A manager owns a lock and a registry, so it cannot be copied or pickled (copy.copy, copy.deepcopy and pickle raise a TypeError): create a new one.

Example 
>>> from minevent import EventManager
>>> def hello_handler():
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> bool(manager)
True
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!

docs.title: minevent.manager.EventManager.add_event_handler
docs.text:
add_event_handler(
    event: str,
    handler: Callable[..., object],
    *,
    once: bool = False,
    condition: Condition | None = None,
) -> Subscription

Add a handler to an event.

The handler will be called every time the specified event is triggered, as handler() or handler(context), where context is the read-only Context built from the payload of the trigger. A parameter that has a default keeps it: the manager never fills it. If no other parameter is left, the handler is called as handler(); if exactly one positional parameter is left, it is called as handler(context); and any other signature is rejected, including *args, **kwargs and a signature that cannot be inspected. This is checked once, at registration, and it never matches names or annotations. Wrap a rejected callable, such as print, in a function or a lambda. Multiple handlers can be registered to the same event, and they will be executed in the order they were added. Use functools.partial to bind other arguments.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default event str

The event name (case-sensitive string) to which the handler should be attached.

required handler Callable[..., object]

The callable to attach to the event.

required once bool

If True, the handler is removed just before its first execution, so it runs at most once, even when several threads trigger the event. A condition that is False does not consume the registration: it waits for the first time the condition is True. Default is False.

False condition Condition | None

An optional condition: a synchronous function that returns a boolean (a condition that returns an awaitable, such as a coroutine function, makes the trigger raise a TypeError). It is called each time the event is triggered, before the handler, and the handler runs only if it returns True. It is called as condition() or condition(context), with the rule of the handlers: a parameter that has a default keeps it. If None, the handler always runs. An exception raised by the condition propagates to the caller of trigger_event. A stateful condition, such as PeriodicCondition, must not be shared between registrations. Default is None.

None

Returns:

Type Description Subscription

A subscription whose remove method removes this registration only.

Raises:

Type Description TypeError

if event is not a string, if handler is not callable, if condition is neither None nor callable, or if handler or condition is a generator function, needs another argument than the context, or has a signature that cannot be inspected. The manager is unchanged.

Example 
>>> import functools
>>> from minevent import EventManager, PeriodicCondition
>>> def hello_handler():
...     print("Hello!")
...
>>> manager = EventManager()
>>> subscription = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> subscription.remove()
True
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("my_event", hello_handler, once=True)
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
Hello!
>>> manager.trigger_event("my_event")
>>> def greet_handler(message):
...     print(message)
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "greet", functools.partial(greet_handler, "Hello!")
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("greet")
Hello!
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler(
...     "tick", hello_handler, condition=PeriodicCondition(freq=2)
... )
>>> manager.trigger_event("tick")
Hello!
>>> manager.trigger_event("tick")
>>> def epoch_handler(context):
...     print(f"epoch {context['epoch']}")
...
>>> _ = manager.add_event_handler("epoch_end", epoch_handler)
>>> manager.trigger_event("epoch_end", {"epoch": 3, "loss": 0.5})
epoch 3
